overview: Mixtec rulers governed several competing kingdoms in southern Mexico, linked by marriages, warfare and trade. The imported “empire” outline is misplaced west of much of the Mixtec heartland; it should not be read as their territorial boundary.

periods.title: Kingdoms and painted histories
periods.summary: Rival dynasties recorded genealogies and political achievements in painted books.

periods.title: Conquest and colonial tribute
periods.summary: Spanish expeditions and alliances reshaped the region; colonial tribute drew on older lordships.

items.text: Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw joined Tilantongo, Teozacoalco and Tututepec under his rule. His story was exceptional within a landscape of competing kingdoms. A powerful ruler could unite several courts without creating one permanent empire for every Mixtec community.

The Tonindeye Codex unfolds like a concertina. Its 47 painted deerskin leaves carry a prepared pale surface and vivid pigments. Fully extended, the book is more than eleven metres long: this family history would not fit across an ordinary kitchen table.

One codex scene shows Lady Five Flint giving birth to an heir, with the child still connected by the umbilical cord. Births and marriages mattered because claims to land and rule depended on relationships between families.

A short reading supplied by the museum is “Iya Nacuaa”, meaning “Lord 8 Deer”. This is a scholarly Latin-script rendering of the ruler’s name represented in the pictorial manuscript, dated 1200 to 1521; its painted signs are not alphabetic letters.

Calendar names linked a person to a day in a 260-day cycle. Animal signs and other images helped identify those days. In 2021, Mixtec researchers used the surviving books together with Indigenous knowledge to reinterpret their communities’ histories.

Excavations at Yucundaa uncovered a palace with patios and rooms reserved for rulers and nobles. Architecture suggests that these spaces combined residence, ritual and formal meetings. For the court, home and workplace could be parts of the same complex.

At that palace, investigators compare doorways, room plans, renovations and refuse from an associated rubbish deposit. Even royal rubbish has something to say: discarded material helps test ideas suggested by impressive walls and painted histories.

Cotton moved between different environments. A historical study describes the inland kingdom of Teozacoalco obtaining it from the coast near Tututepec. A cloth’s story could therefore begin in warm coastal fields and continue in workshops far inland.

A Mixtec gold necklace in the Met has beads shaped like jaguar teeth. Its delicate loops were modeled in wax and cast in metal, a technique called false filigree. What looks like tiny bent wires could begin as a carefully shaped wax model.

The museum compares this necklace with objects excavated in Monte Albán’s Tomb 7. That tomb contained mixed remains of men, women and children, suggesting reuse or secondary burial. Its riches cannot securely identify one famous king as the principal occupant.

Spanish conquest in Oaxaca involved rival local alliances as well as armed expeditions. Some Zapotec rulers sought help against Tututepec; other communities resisted. These choices had local purposes, even as Spanish rule brought new forms of domination.

Ancient DNA from ten people buried at Teposcolula-Yucundaa identified Salmonella Paratyphi C. Researchers propose it as a strong candidate behind the local 1545 epidemic. Teeth preserved evidence that could help investigate a catastrophe centuries after the people died.

ending.text: Spanish rule and colonial tribute transformed Mixtec kingdoms during the sixteenth century; the imported 1530 cutoff is not one empire’s fall. Mixtec peoples, languages and historical traditions continue, and Indigenous scholars actively interpret the surviving books.
